title: The Two-Way Street
description: Interactive simulation of a cohort of 500 fictional people with gut-symptom and mood-symptom scores. Learners set the strength of gut-to-brain effects, brain-to-gut effects, and a shared confounding factor, then compare the correlation from one snapshot with time-lagged correlations from following the cohort over time.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Explain why a gut-to-brain effect, a brain-to-gut effect, or a shared third factor can each produce a similar gut-mood correlation at one time point.
Analyze how following people over time helps detect the direction of an effect (reverse causation) but cannot by itself rule out confounding.
prerequisites: Basic idea of anxiety and depression symptoms
keyQuestions: Can one survey of gut and mood symptoms show which causes which?
What does it mean if earlier gut symptoms predict later mood?
What if effects run in both directions?
How can a hidden third factor create a correlation?
misconceptions: A correlation between gut problems and anxiety proves the gut causes anxiety.
If anxiety is linked to IBD, anxiety must cause IBD.
Following people over time removes every possible confounder.
Effects can only run in one direction.
